claims.claim: Silencing SLs did not alter PYR odor responses.
claims.source: Notably, silencing SLs did not alter PYR odor responses
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figures 2 and 3.

claims.claim: SLs and PYRs exhibited differences in odor tuning properties and response discriminability.
claims.source: SLs and PYRs exhibited differences in odor tuning properties and response discriminability that were consistent with their distinct embeddings within a sensory-associative cortex.
claims.evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claims.claim: SLs and PYRs form parallel channels for differentially processing odor information in and through PCx.
claims.source: Our results therefore suggest that SLs and PYRs form parallel channels for differentially processing odor information in and through PCx.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from the experimental results presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: Superficial pyramidal (PYR) cells in deeper layer II receive afferent olfactory bulb (OB) inputs on their distal apical dendrites.
claims.source: Superficial pyramidal (PYR) cells in deeper layer II receive afferent olfactory bulb (OB) inputs on their distal apical dendrites, dense excitatory intracortical inputs on their proximal apical dendrites, and top-down inputs from other brain regions on their basal dendrites.
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by the citations provided (Heimer and Kalil, 1978; Haberly, 1983; Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013).

claims.claim: Semilunar (SL) cells in superficial layer II receive strong OB inputs on their distal apical dendrites.
claims.source: By contrast, semilunar (SL) cells in superficial layer II receive strong OB inputs on their distal apical dendrites, few, if any, excitatory intracortical inputs, and lack basal dendrites (Figure 1a; Heimer and Kalil, 1978; Haberly, 1983; Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations and illustrated in Figure 1a.

claims.claim: SL cells receive few, if any, excitatory intracortical inputs.
claims.source: By contrast, semilunar (SL) cells in superficial layer II receive strong OB inputs on their distal apical dendrites, few, if any, excitatory intracortical inputs, and lack basal dendrites (Figure 1a; Heimer and Kalil, 1978; Haberly, 1983; Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from prior literature as indicated by the citations.

claims.claim: SL cells lack basal dendrites.
claims.source: By contrast, semilunar (SL) cells in superficial layer II receive strong OB inputs on their distal apical dendrites, few, if any, excitatory intracortical inputs, and lack basal dendrites (Figure 1a; Heimer and Kalil, 1978; Haberly, 1983; Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge supported by citations.

claims.claim: SLs and PYRs project to distinct downstream regions.
claims.source: That SLs and PYRs project to distinct downstream regions (Diodato et al., 2016; Mazo et al., 2017) lends support to a parallel model.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: SLs responded 2–4 ms earlier than PYRs following electrical stimulation of OB mitral cell axons in the lateral olfactory tract (LOT).
claims.source: Support for this sequential model stems from observations that SLs receive stronger OB inputs than PYRs but little or no intracortical excitatory inputs, and that SLs respond 2–4 ms earlier than PYRs following electrical stimulation of OB mitral cell axons in the lateral olfactory tract (LOT) (Ketchum and Haberly, 1993; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2006; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2011; Wiegand et al., 2011; Choy et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from prior studies as indicated by the citations.

claims.claim: In PCx, Cre-expressing cells were largely restricted to the superficial half of layer II (i.e., layer IIa), where SLs are located.
claims.source: In PCx, Cre-expressing cells were largely restricted to the superficial half of layer II (i.e., layer IIa), where SLs are located (Figure 1b).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data shown in Figure 1b.

claims.claim: 87.9% ± 3.54% of Ntng1+ cells displayed hallmark morphological characteristics of SLs.
claims.source: Ntng1+ cells displayed hallmark morphological characteristics of SLs: half-moon-shaped somata, two prominent apical dendrites emerging directly from the cell body and no basal dendrites (percent Ntng1+ cells with SL morphology, mean ± SD: 87.9% ± 3.54%, n = 3 mice; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Ntng1+ and Ntng1- cells exhibited the intrinsic biophysical properties described in SLs and PYRs, respectively.
claims.source: Additionally, Ntng1+ and Ntng1- cells exhibited the intrinsic biophysical properties described in SLs and PYRs, respectively (Figure 1c–h; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2006; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1c-h and comparison to prior literature.

claims.claim: Ntng1+ cells make glutamatergic synapses onto Ntng1- cells.
claims.source: These light-evoked responses were completely blocked by glutamate receptor antagonists (NBQX and CPP) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3b). Thus, Ntng1+ cells make glutamatergic synapses onto Ntng1- cells, but not onto other Ntng1+ cells, consistent with the synaptic connectivity of SLs and PYRs.
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3b showing pharmacological blockade.

claims.claim: Ntng1+ cells do not make glutamatergic synapses onto other Ntng1+ cells.
claims.source: Thus, Ntng1+ cells make glutamatergic synapses onto Ntng1- cells, but not onto other Ntng1+ cells, consistent with the synaptic connectivity of SLs and PYRs.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing minimal light-evoked currents in Ntng1+ cells when Ntng1+ cells expressing ChR2 were activated.

claims.claim: SLs receive some intracortical excitatory inputs from other PCx neurons, although these were 5.4× weaker than inputs received by PYRs.
claims.source: Interestingly, we now observed small inward currents in SLs, indicating that SLs do receive some intracortical excitatory inputs from other PCx neurons, although these were 5.4× weaker than inputs received by PYRs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3g and h).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3g and h.

claims.claim: SLs had higher spontaneous spike rates than PYRs (median SL: 1.99 Hz, n = 426 cells; median PYR: 1.03 Hz, n = 464 cells; p=5.08 × 10–13).
claims.source: SLs had higher spontaneous spike rates than PYRs (median SL: 1.99 Hz, n = 426 cells; median PYR: 1.03 Hz, n = 464 cells; p=5.08 × 10–13, unpaired t-test; Figure 1l)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 1l.

claims.claim: During light-on trials, odor-evoked activity was markedly suppressed in SLs but remained unchanged in PYRs.
claims.source: During light-on trials, odor-evoked activity, measured as response peaks in a 300 ms period after odor inhalation, was markedly suppressed in SLs but remained unchanged in PYRs (Figure 2f and g).
claims.evidence: This is a primary experimental finding supported by data in Figure 2f and g.

claims.claim: Median peak firing rate for significantly activated SL responses was 29.7 Hz during light-off and 13.0 Hz during light-on (n = 101 cell-odor pairs; p=2.71 × 10–12).
claims.source: This was the case when we only considered robustly activated responses (median peak firing rate for significantly activated responses [p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test]: SL, light-off: 29.7 Hz, light-on: 13.0 Hz; n = 101 cell-odor pairs; p=2.71 × 10–12, paired t-test; PYR, light-off: 24.9 Hz, light-on: 28.2 Hz; n = 97 cell-odor pairs; p=0.234; Figure 2h)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 2h.

claims.claim: Median peak firing rate for significantly activated PYR responses was 24.9 Hz during light-off and 28.2 Hz during light-on (n = 97 cell-odor pairs; p=0.234).
claims.source: This was the case when we only considered robustly activated responses (median peak firing rate for significantly activated responses [p<0.05, Wilcoxon rank-sum test]: SL, light-off: 29.7 Hz, light-on: 13.0 Hz; n = 101 cell-odor pairs; p=2.71 × 10–12, paired t-test; PYR, light-off: 24.9 Hz, light-on: 28.2 Hz; n = 97 cell-odor pairs; p=0.234; Figure 2h)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 2h.

claims.claim: SL response patterns across odors were significantly altered in the light-on trials compared to the light-off (off-off, 0.895 [0.888, 0.901]; on-off, 0.583 [0.526, 0.633]; unpaired t-test, p=5.10 × 10–6).
claims.source: SL response patterns across odors were significantly altered in the light-on trials compared to the light-off (off-off, 0.895 [0.888, 0.901]; on-off, 0.583 [0.526, 0.633]; unpaired t-test, p=5.10 × 10–6; Figure 2j)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 2j.

claims.claim: PYR response patterns were unchanged between light-on and light-off conditions (off-off, 0.834 [0.816, 0.861]; on-off, 0.838 [0.792, 0.876]; unpaired t-test, p=0.882).
claims.source: while PYR response patterns were unchanged (off-off, 0.834 [0.816, 0.861]; on-off, 0.838 [0.792, 0.876]; unpaired t-test, p=0.882).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data.

claims.claim: Odor identity decoding within each condition revealed a substantial decrease in SL performance in the light-on condition (p=0.0116), with no change in PYR performance (p=0.919).
claims.source: Odor identity decoding within each condition revealed a substantial decrease in SL performance in the light-on condition, with no change in PYR performance (SL, p=0.0116; PYR, p=0.919, paired t-test; Figure 2k and l).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from decoding analysis shown in Figure 2k and l.

claims.claim: Following administration of CNO/C21, there was a gradual and marked decrease in SL spontaneous activity and a concomitant small decrease in PYR spontaneous activity.
claims.source: Following administration of the DREADD agonists, CNO or Compound 21 (C21), we observed a gradual and marked decrease in SL spontaneous activity and a concomitant small decrease in PYR spontaneous activity (Figure 3c).
claims.evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 3c.

claims.claim: Odor-evoked response peaks in SLs were lower after CNO/C21 injection (median peak firing rate: SL, baseline: 14.8 Hz, CNO/C21: 6.38 Hz; n = 124 cell-odor pairs; paired t-test, p=0.0086).
claims.source: This was the case for both robustly activated responses (median peak firing rate: SL, baseline: 14.8 Hz, CNO/C21: 6.38 Hz; n = 124 cell-odor pairs; paired t-test, p=0.0086; PYR, baseline: 18.5 Hz, CNO/C21: 17.1 Hz; p=0.0338; n = 96 cell-odor pairs; Figure 3f)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claims.claim: PYR odor-evoked response peaks were largely unaffected after CNO/C21 injection (median peak firing rate: PYR, baseline: 18.5 Hz, CNO/C21: 17.1 Hz; p=0.0338; n = 96 cell-odor pairs).
claims.source: This was the case for both robustly activated responses (median peak firing rate: SL, baseline: 14.8 Hz, CNO/C21: 6.38 Hz; n = 124 cell-odor pairs; paired t-test, p=0.0086; PYR, baseline: 18.5 Hz, CNO/C21: 17.1 Hz; p=0.0338; n = 96 cell-odor pairs; Figure 3f)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3f.

claims.claim: SL responses measured before and after CNO/C21 were markedly different (baseline-baseline, 0.944 [0.920, 0.953]; CNO/C21-baseline, 0.300 [0.220, 0.393]; p=1.46 × 10–7).
claims.source: Responses measured before and after CNO/C21 were markedly different in SLs (baseline-baseline, 0.944 [0.920, 0.953]; CNO/C21-baseline, 0.300 [0.220, 0.393]; p=1.46 × 10–7, unpaired t-test; Figure 3h).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3h.

claims.claim: PYR responses also changed after CNO/C21 administration (baseline-baseline, 0.950 [0.913, 0.968]; CNO/C21-baseline, 0.729 [0.7, 0.759]; p=2.53 × 10–6).
claims.source: PYR responses also changed after CNO/C21 administration (baseline-baseline, 0.950 [0.913, 0.968]; CNO/C21-baseline, 0.729 [0.7, 0.759]; p=2.53 × 10–6; Figure 3h)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 3h.

claims.claim: The distributions of response latencies of SLs and PYRs were similar (median latency to peak: SL, 59.0 ms; PYR, 57.0 ms; Wilcoxon rank-sum test: p=0.199).
claims.source: In both measures, the distributions of response latencies of SLs and PYRs were similar (median latency to peak: SL, 59.0 ms; PYR, 57.0 ms; Wilcoxon rank-sum test: p=0.199; median onset latency: SL, 38.2 ms; PYR, 38.2 ms; Wilcoxon rank-sum test: p=0.587, Figure 4b and d).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 4b and d.

claims.claim: Median onset latency for SLs was 38.2 ms and for PYRs was 38.2 ms (Wilcoxon rank-sum test: p=0.587).
claims.source: In both measures, the distributions of response latencies of SLs and PYRs were similar (median latency to peak: SL, 59.0 ms; PYR, 57.0 ms; Wilcoxon rank-sum test: p=0.199; median onset latency: SL, 38.2 ms; PYR, 38.2 ms; Wilcoxon rank-sum test: p=0.587, Figure 4b and d).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 4b and d.

claims.claim: SLs had slightly more suppressed odor responses than PYRs.
claims.source: Both cell types exhibited similar patterns of odor-activated and -suppressed responses but SLs had slightly more suppressed odor responses than PYRs (Figure 5a and b), likely due, in part, to their higher baseline firing rates.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from experimental data shown in Figure 5a and b, with an inference about the cause.

claims.claim: SLs had significantly lower lifetime sparseness values than PYRs (mean lifetime sparseness: SL, 0.434 [0.414, 0.458], n = 426 cells; PYR, 0.558 [0.536, 0.581], n = 464 cells; p=2.61 × 10–14).
claims.source: SLs had significantly lower lifetime sparseness values than PYRs, indicating that SLs are less odor selective than PYRs (mean lifetime sparseness: SL, 0.434 [0.414, 0.458], n = 426 cells; PYR, 0.558 [0.536, 0.581], n = 464 cells; p=2.61 × 10–14, unpaired t-test; Figure 5c).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5c.

claims.claim: The SL population response to each odor was significantly less sparse than the PYR population response (SL, 0.686 [0.681, 0.691]; PYR, 0.755 [0.737, 0.771]; n = 10 odors; p=1.61 × 10–6).
claims.source: The SL population response to each odor was significantly less sparse than the PYR population response (SL, 0.686 [0.681, 0.691]; PYR, 0.755 [0.737, 0.771]; n = 10 odors; p=1.61 × 10–6, unpaired t-test; Figure 5d).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5d.

claims.claim: Response reliability was similar between SLs and PYRs (SL, 0.474 [0.452, 0.497]; PYR, 0.499 [0.472, 0.525]; n = 10 odors; p=0.191).
claims.source: By this metric, response reliability was similar between SLs and PYRs (SL, 0.474 [0.452, 0.497]; PYR, 0.499 [0.472, 0.525]; n = 10 odors; p=0.191, unpaired t-test)
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data.

claims.claim: Odors were slightly more discriminable in PYR responses (SL, 0.266 [0.254, 0.279]; PYR, 0.238 [0.220, 0.253]; p=0.0193).
claims.source: but odors were slightly more discriminable in PYR responses (SL, 0.266 [0.254, 0.279]; PYR, 0.238 [0.220, 0.253]; p=0.0193; Figure 5f).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5f.

claims.claim: Odors were more separable in PYR responses than in SL responses (median distance: SL, 19.4; PYR, 27.4; n = 45 odor pairs; p=3.21 × 10–7).
claims.source: We quantified the Euclidean distances between the means of the first six principal components of pairs of odors and found that odors were more separable in PYR responses than in SL responses (median distance: SL, 19.4; PYR, 27.4; n = 45 odor pairs; p=3.21 × 10–7, unpaired t-test; Figure 5h).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 5h.

claims.claim: Odor classification accuracy, at all pseudopopulation sizes, was similar in SLs and PYRs.
claims.source: Finally, we asked if a downstream decoder could more accurately identify odors based on PYR versus SL odor-evoked activity. However, odor classification accuracy, at all pseudopopulation sizes, was similar in SLs and PYRs (Figure 5i, left).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from decoding analysis shown in Figure 5i.

claims.claim: The Ntng1Cre mouse line expresses Cre-recombinase in a subpopulation of PCx principal neurons whose laminar, morphological, intrinsic, and local connectivity properties are congruent with those of SLs.
claims.source: Taken together, the Ntng1Cre mouse expresses Cre-recombinase in a subpopulation of PCx principal neurons whose laminar, morphological, intrinsic, and local connectivity properties are congruent with those of SLs.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations presented in the manuscript.

claims.claim: SLs preferentially project to the posterior PCx, posteromedial cortical amygdala, and lateral entorhinal cortex.
claims.source: Interestingly, SLs preferentially project to the posterior PCx, posteromedial cortical amygdala, and lateral entorhinal cortex while PYRs project back to the OB, medial prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortices (Diodato et al., 2016; Mazo et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: PYRs project back to the OB, medial prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortices.
claims.source: Interestingly, SLs preferentially project to the posterior PCx, posteromedial cortical amygdala, and lateral entorhinal cortex while PYRs project back to the OB, medial prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortices (Diodato et al., 2016; Mazo et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Inputs onto PYRs from other PYRs are approximately five times stronger than inputs from SLs.
claims.source: Inputs onto PYRs from other PYRs are approximately five times stronger than inputs from SLs (Figure 1—figure supplement 3e and h).
claims.evidence: This is a quantitative finding from experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3e and h.

claims.claim: Resting membrane potentials of Ntng1+ cells were –65.4 mV [–70,–60] (n = 11 cells) and Ntng1- cells were –77.0 mV [–80.6,–72.9] (n = 7 cells; p=5.27 × 10–4).
claims.source: (e) Resting membrane potentials of Ntng1+ and Ntng1- cells (Ntng1+: –65.4 mV [–70,–60], n = 11 cells; Ntng1-: –77.0 mV [–80.6,–72.9], n = 7 cells; p=5.27 × 10–4, unpaired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 1e.

claims.claim: Input resistances of Ntng1+ cells were 541 MΩ [415, 669] (n = 9 cells) and Ntng1- cells were 166 MΩ [104, 243] (n = 8 cells; p=2.15 × 10–4).
claims.source: (f) Input resistances of Ntng1+ and Ntng1- cells (Ntng1+: 541 MΩ [415, 669], n = 9 cells; Ntng1-: 166 MΩ [104, 243], n = 8 cells; p=2.15 × 10–4, unpaired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 1f.

claims.claim: Membrane time constants of Ntng1+ cells were 32.1 ms [27.7, 35.8] (n = 11 cells) and Ntng1- cells were 13.6 ms [11.2, 16.0] (n = 8 cells; p=1.29 × 10–5).
claims.source: (g) Membrane time constants of Ntng1+ and Ntng1- cells (Ntng1+: 32.1 ms [27.7, 35.8], n = 11 cells; Ntng1-: 13.6 ms [11.2, 16.0], n = 8 cells; p=1.29 × 10–5, unpaired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 1g.

claims.claim: Burst indices of Ntng1+ cells were 1.16 [0.926, 1.41] (n = 8 cells) and Ntng1- cells were 4.57 [3.12, 6.19] (n = 8 cells; p=1.43 × 10–4).
claims.source: (h) Burst indices of Ntng1+ and Ntng1- cells (Ntng1+: 1.16 [0.926, 1.41], n = 8 cells; Ntng1-: 4.57 [3.12, 6.19], n = 8 cells; p=1.43 × 10–4, unpaired t-test).
claims.evidence: This is a statistical finding from experimental data shown in Figure 1h.

claims.claim: PCx is a three-layered allocortex with principal neurons primarily located in layer II.
claims.source: Piriform cortex (PCx) is a three-layered allocortex with principal neurons primarily located in layer II.
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about PCx.

claims.claim: Individual PCx neurons integrate convergent inputs from different combinations of glomeruli.
claims.source: Individual PCx neurons integrate convergent inputs from different combinations of glomeruli (Apicella et al., 2010; Davison and Ehlers, 2011).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: SLs almost exclusively receive afferent OB inputs.
claims.source: SLs almost exclusively receive afferent OB inputs, while PYRs receive both afferent OB inputs and dense intracortical inputs from SLs and other PYRs (Johnson et al., 2000; Franks et al., 2011; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2011; Hagiwara et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: PYRs receive both afferent OB inputs and dense intracortical inputs from SLs and other PYRs.
claims.source: SLs almost exclusively receive afferent OB inputs, while PYRs receive both afferent OB inputs and dense intracortical inputs from SLs and other PYRs (Johnson et al., 2000; Franks et al., 2011; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2011; Hagiwara et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: Odor responses in layer III of PCx were more correlated between chemically similar odor stimuli than responses in layer II or the OB.
claims.source: A recent study showed that odor responses in layer III of PCx, which only contains PYRs, were more correlated between chemically similar odor stimuli than responses in layer II, which contain both SLs and PYRs, or the OB (Pashkovski et al., 2020)
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a prior study as indicated by the citation.

claims.claim: Cells in the ventral telencephalon (Vv) of zebrafish receive primarily OB inputs and exhibit broader stimulus tuning and more overlapping odor representations than those in the dorsal telencephalon (Dp).
claims.source: Our findings on the stimulus selectivity and discriminability of SLs and PYRs are also comparable to those reported in two zebrafish odor centers downstream of the OB: cells in the ventral telencephalon (Vv) receive primarily OB inputs and exhibit broader stimulus tuning and more overlapping odor representations than those in the dorsal telencephalon (Dp), which is the teleost homolog of PCx (Yaksi et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a prior study as indicated by the citation.

claims.claim: The dorsal telencephalon (Dp) in zebrafish is the teleost homolog of PCx.
claims.source: Our findings on the stimulus selectivity and discriminability of SLs and PYRs are also comparable to those reported in two zebrafish odor centers downstream of the OB: cells in the ventral telencephalon (Vv) receive primarily OB inputs and exhibit broader stimulus tuning and more overlapping odor representations than those in the dorsal telencephalon (Dp), which is the teleost homolog of PCx (Yaksi et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claims.claim: Different mitral cells respond to odors with variable latencies that tile the entire ~300 ms sniff cycle.
claims.source: However, different mitral cells respond to odors with variable latencies that tile the entire ~300 ms sniff cycle (Cury and Uchida, 2010; Shusterman et al., 2011; Bolding and Franks, 2018)
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: PCx spans ~4 mm along its anterior-posterior axis.
claims.source: However, PCx spans ~4 mm along its anterior-posterior axis and is a long-range recurrent network with neurons forming intracortical connections with neurons >1 mm away (Johnson et al., 2000; Franks et al., 2011; Hagiwara et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is an anatomical measurement supported by citations.

claims.claim: PCx is a long-range recurrent network with neurons forming intracortical connections with neurons >1 mm away.
claims.source: However, PCx spans ~4 mm along its anterior-posterior axis and is a long-range recurrent network with neurons forming intracortical connections with neurons >1 mm away (Johnson et al., 2000; Franks et al., 2011; Hagiwara et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: PCx and the hippocampus are analogous structures.
claims.source: PCx and the hippocampus are analogous structures.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative statement based on structural and functional similarities.

claims.claim: Both PCx and hippocampus are trilaminar paleocortices with extensive recurrent networks that support unsupervised learning.
claims.source: Both are trilaminar paleocortices with extensive recurrent networks (Guzman et al., 2016) that support unsupervised learning (Barkai et al., 1994; Haberly, 2001; Rolls, 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claims.claim: In terms of morphology and connectivity, PYRs are analogous to CA3 pyramidal cells and SLs to dentate gyrus (DG) granule cells.
claims.source: In terms of morphology and connectivity, PYRs are analogous to CA3 pyramidal cells and SLs to dentate gyrus (DG) granule cells.
claims.evidence: This is a comparative statement based on structural similarities.

claims.claim: DG granule cells are thought to drive the acquisition of memories, but not retrieval, and perform pattern separation.
claims.source: The roles of DG and CA3 in the encoding of episodic memories are relatively well characterized; DG granule cells are thought to drive the acquisition of memories, but not retrieval, and perform pattern separation while CA3 pyramidal cells are thought to store and retrieve memories and perform pattern completion (Leutgeb et al., 2007; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014; Madar et al., 2019; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from hippocampal research supported by citations.

claims.claim: CA3 pyramidal cells are thought to store and retrieve memories and perform pattern completion.
claims.source: The roles of DG and CA3 in the encoding of episodic memories are relatively well characterized; DG granule cells are thought to drive the acquisition of memories, but not retrieval, and perform pattern separation while CA3 pyramidal cells are thought to store and retrieve memories and perform pattern completion (Leutgeb et al., 2007; Neunuebel and Knierim, 2014; Madar et al., 2019; Hainmueller and Bartos, 2020).
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from hippocampal research supported by citations.

claims.claim: When DG projections to CA3 are silenced or ablated, the ability of CA3 to retrieve memories is unimpaired.
claims.source: It is important to note that although DG granule cells synapse onto CA3 pyramidal cells, the DG-CA3 circuit is not exclusively sequential. CA3 also receives direct input from the entorhinal cortex, and when DG projections to CA3 are silenced or ablated, the ability of CA3 to retrieve memories is unimpaired (Lee and Kesner, 2004).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a prior study as indicated by the citation.

claims.claim: PYRs were more robust to degraded afferent OB inputs and exhibited more persistent odor-evoked activity after stimulus offset than SLs.
claims.source: In our previous study with the Ntng1Cre mouse line, we found that PYRs were more robust to degraded afferent OB inputs and exhibited more persistent odor-evoked activity after stimulus offset than SLs (Bolding et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the authors as indicated by the citation.

claims.claim: Only 7% of all recorded PCx neurons, and fewer than 1% of layer II PCx neurons, were GABAergic inhibitory neurons.
claims.source: We previously found that only 7% of all recorded PCx neurons, and fewer than 1% of layer II PCx neurons, were GABAergic inhibitory neurons (Bolding and Franks, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is a finding from a prior study by the authors as indicated by the citation.

claims.claim: Odor representations in PCx do not appear to encode odor value or be task-specific.
claims.source: However, this seems unlikely given recent evidence that odor representations in PCx do not appear to encode odor value or be task-specific (Gadziola et al., 2020; Millman and Murthy, 2020; Wang et al., 2020)

results.result: The Ntng1Cre mouse line selectively labels semilunar (SL) cells in piriform cortex layer IIa with appropriate morphological, laminar, and biophysical properties. Ntng1+ cells showed SL-characteristic morphology (87.9% ± 3.54%), were restricted to layer IIa, and exhibited distinct biophysical properties compared to Ntng1- cells including more depolarized resting potentials, higher input resistance, longer time constants, and lower burst indices.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C14 and C39 provide converging anatomical and morphological evidence, while C43-C46 provide quantitative biophysical measurements with appropriate statistical tests (all p<0.001). The data demonstrate that the Ntng1Cre line is a valid genetic tool for targeting SLs, which is foundational for all subsequent experiments.

results.result: SLs make glutamatergic synapses onto PYRs but not onto other SLs, and receive weak intracortical excitatory inputs. Optogenetic activation of Ntng1+ cells evoked glutamate receptor-dependent responses in PYRs but minimal responses in other SLs. When all PCx neurons were activated, SLs received intracortical inputs that were 5.4× weaker than those received by PYRs, and PYR-to-PYR connections were ~5× stronger than SL-to-PYR connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C17 and C42 are supported by pharmacological validation (complete blockade by NBQX/CPP) and quantitative measurements from voltage-clamp recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3. The connectivity pattern is consistent with prior literature and validates the functional properties of the Ntng1Cre-labeled cells.

results.result: Optogenetic suppression of SLs markedly reduced SL odor responses but did not alter PYR odor responses or population response patterns. During light-on trials, SL median peak firing decreased from 29.7 Hz to 13.0 Hz (p=2.71×10⁻¹²), while PYR responses remained unchanged (24.9 Hz vs 28.2 Hz, p=0.234). SL response patterns were significantly altered (correlation: 0.895 vs 0.583, p=5.10×10⁻⁶), but PYR patterns were unchanged (0.834 vs 0.838, p=0.882).
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C19-C24 present the core optogenetic manipulation result with appropriate statistical tests and controls. The data convincingly show that PYR odor responses are independent of SL activity, contradicting the sequential processing model. Sample sizes are adequate (n=9 experiments, 101 SL and 97 PYR cell-odor pairs) and the effect sizes are substantial for SLs but absent for PYRs.

results.result: Chemogenetic suppression of SLs using hm4di/CNO confirmed that PYR odor responses are largely independent of SL input. CNO/C21 administration caused gradual suppression of SL spontaneous and odor-evoked activity (baseline: 14.8 Hz, CNO: 6.38 Hz, p=0.0086), while PYR responses were minimally affected (baseline: 18.5 Hz, CNO: 17.1 Hz, p=0.0338). SL response patterns changed dramatically (correlation: 0.944 vs 0.300, p=1.46×10⁻⁷), while PYR changes were smaller (0.950 vs 0.729, p=2.53×10⁻⁶) and comparable to control conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C29 provide chemogenetic validation of the optogenetic findings with appropriate controls (mCherry/Arch without CNO, and mCherry/Arch with CNO). The temporal confound (30 min between baseline and CNO conditions) is acknowledged and controlled for. The effect on PYRs in the experimental group was not significantly different from controls (p=0.491), supporting independence of PYR responses from SL input.

results.result: SLs and PYRs exhibited similar odor response latencies. Median latency to peak was 59.0 ms for SLs and 57.0 ms for PYRs (p=0.199), and median onset latency was 38.2 ms for both cell types (p=0.587).
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 are supported by quantitative latency measurements from a large dataset (n=15 experiments, 1352 SL and 1305 PYR cell-odor pairs for peak latency). The statistical tests are appropriate (Wilcoxon rank-sum) and show no significant difference. This contradicts the sequential model prediction that SLs should respond earlier than PYRs, though the authors acknowledge limitations of latency analysis in awake animals.

results.result: SLs and PYRs exhibit distinct odor tuning properties. SLs were less odor-selective (lifetime sparseness: 0.434 vs 0.558, p=2.61×10⁻¹⁴), had less sparse population responses (0.686 vs 0.755, p=1.61×10⁻⁶), and odors were more discriminable in PYRs (correlation between odors: 0.266 vs 0.238, p=0.0193; Euclidean distance: 19.4 vs 27.4, p=3.21×10⁻⁷). However, response reliability was similar (0.474 vs 0.499, p=0.191) and odor classification accuracy was equivalent at all population sizes.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C38 provide comprehensive characterization of odor response properties with appropriate statistical tests and large sample sizes (426 SLs, 464 PYRs). The findings are internally consistent: SLs are more broadly tuned and less sparse, while PYRs show better discriminability. The lack of difference in decoding accuracy despite differences in discriminability is surprising but honestly reported. The data support the parallel processing model with differential encoding.

results.result: SLs and PYRs form parallel channels for differentially processing odor information in and through PCx, rather than operating in a sequential hierarchy.
results.evaluation: Claim C5 represents the main conclusion, which is well-supported by the convergence of multiple lines of evidence: (1) PYR responses are independent of SL activity (C3, C19-C29), (2) response latencies are similar (C30-C31), (3) tuning properties differ in ways consistent with their connectivity (C32-C37), and (4) both cell types project to distinct downstream targets (C10, C40-C41). The parallel processing model is more consistent with the data than the sequential model.

results.result: PCx contains two main types of principal neurons (SLs and PYRs) with distinct anatomical properties. PCx is a three-layered allocortex with principal neurons in layer II. PYRs receive OB inputs on distal apical dendrites, intracortical inputs on proximal apical dendrites, and top-down inputs on basal dendrites. SLs receive strong OB inputs on distal apical dendrites, few intracortical inputs, and lack basal dendrites.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C6-C9 describe established anatomical knowledge supported by multiple citations (Heimer and Kalil, 1978; Haberly, 1983; Bekkers and Suzuki, 2013). This provides essential background context for the study. C47 is basic anatomical knowledge about PCx structure.

results.result: SLs and PYRs project to distinct downstream regions and show differential response timing in slice preparations. SLs project to posterior PCx, posteromedial cortical amygdala, and lateral entorhinal cortex, while PYRs project to OB, medial prefrontal and orbitofrontal cortices. In slice experiments with LOT stimulation, SLs responded 2-4 ms earlier than PYRs.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C11 and C40-C41 cite prior literature (Diodato et al., 2016; Mazo et al., 2017; Ketchum and Haberly, 1993; Suzuki and Bekkers, 2006, 2011; Wiegand et al., 2011; Choy et al., 2017). These establish the anatomical basis for the parallel processing hypothesis and provide context for why the sequential model was previously favored. The authors' in vivo latency data (C30-C31) contradict the slice-based latency findings.

results.result: SLs had higher spontaneous spike rates than PYRs (median: 1.99 Hz vs 1.03 Hz, p=5.08×10⁻¹³).
results.evaluation: Claim C18 is a straightforward quantitative finding with appropriate statistics and large sample sizes (426 SLs, 464 PYRs). This validates that the recording and cell identification methods can resolve differences between cell types. Higher spontaneous rates in SLs may contribute to their higher suppressed odor responses (C32).

results.result: Prior studies have established that PCx neurons integrate convergent glomerular inputs, SLs primarily receive OB inputs while PYRs receive both OB and intracortical inputs, layer III PYR responses are more correlated for similar odors, zebrafish olfactory centers show analogous organization, mitral cells respond with variable latencies across the sniff cycle, and PCx is a long-range recurrent network spanning ~4 mm.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C56 cite relevant prior literature that provides context for interpreting the current findings. These are appropriately cited background claims that help frame the discussion of results. The citations appear accurate based on the references provided.

results.result: PCx and hippocampus are analogous structures with similar organization. Both are trilaminar paleocortices with recurrent networks supporting unsupervised learning. PYRs are analogous to CA3 pyramidal cells and SLs to DG granule cells. In hippocampus, DG drives memory acquisition and pattern separation while CA3 stores/retrieves memories and performs pattern completion. CA3 memory retrieval is unimpaired when DG projections are silenced. Previous work showed PYRs are more robust to degraded OB input than SLs.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C63 draw analogies between PCx and hippocampus based on structural and functional similarities, supported by appropriate citations. The analogy is used to interpret the parallel-loop organization and the independence of PYR responses from SL input (similar to CA3 independence from DG for retrieval). C63 cites the authors' prior work (Bolding et al., 2020). The analogies are reasonable but speculative regarding functional roles.

results.result: Only 7% of recorded PCx neurons were GABAergic inhibitory neurons, and odor representations in PCx do not encode odor value or appear task-specific.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C65 cite prior work to support methodological decisions (justifying classification of non-SL units as PYRs) and to argue against task-dependent explanations for the findings. The citations appear appropriate (Bolding and Franks, 2018; Gadziola et al., 2020; Millman and Murthy, 2020; Wang et al., 2020).
